request.text:
Can't, or won't?
<long pause>
I'm coming with you to the Keep. If anyone hears that verse sung at last, it's going to be me.
<long pause>
Pay it back, children, or pay what you've known.
<long pause>
Twenty years. And it was sitting in a tower all along, waiting for someone to ask.
<long pause>
Whatever you choose up there, every square in the Vale will know what the choice was. I'll make sure of it.
<long pause>
Ah, an audience! Stand there and look grave, and I'll sing you something the Wardens wrote before your grandmothers were born.
<long pause>
Look at you. Still holding a lute like it owes you money.
<long pause>
I left because the songs were moving, and a songkeeper has to move with them. I should have said goodbye. We're terrible at endings. We always think there's another verse.
<long pause>
Stay close this time. If the songs are right, the Vale is about to need someone who can tell the whole of it.
<long pause>
Seven went over the Greywall high, and seven came home with a fire in the sky. The Wardens kept it and the Wardens sang, and the whole Vale warmed where the hearth-bells rang.
<long pause>
That's the Wardens' Song of the Seven. Seven went, seven came home, a gift and a hearth and everyone happy.
<long pause>
There's a last verse, too. Nobody has sung it in two hundred years. When a song loses its last verse on purpose, it's usually because the last verse was true.
<long pause>
Songs gather where things are about to happen. A starving town, a goblin on a bridge, an ember going cold under the river. This is the best stage in the Vale.
<long pause>
And someone I've been following came this way. Never mind who. That's a song for later, somewhere colder.
<long pause>
Anything else? I take requests. I don't take criticism.
<long pause>
Go on, then. Do something worth a verse.
<long pause>
The bridge ballad's a sad one now. They always are, when you write them honestly.
<long pause>
A truce at the ford! I'll need a whole new verse. Possibly three.
